input_signals.name: LeverageWeightedGrossProfit
input_signals.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(SUB(revt, ADD(cogs, xsga)), at)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(wcap, at)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Because equity is a residual claim, one unit of operating profitability moves equity value far more when the firm carries heavy liabilities and a thin working-capital buffer; investors underreact to this leverage-amplified information, so profitability earns its largest premium exactly where distress exposure is greatest.
input_signals.reasoning: The critique was that a z-scored leverage multiplier flips sign for low-leverage firms and pooled unprofitable-unlevered names into the long leg; replacing it with a strictly non-negative distress weight (rank of a leverage plus working-capital-deficiency composite in [0,1]) makes the signal monotone in profitability at every leverage level and near zero for the safest firms. The long leg is therefore unambiguously profitable-and-stressed and the short leg unprofitable-and-stressed, which is the interaction the hypothesis describes rather than either main effect.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_zscore( ratio( sub( revt, add( cogs, xsga ) ), at ) ), rank( sumrank( ratio( lt, at ), neg( ratio( wcap, at ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: WorstCaseObligationCoverage
input_signals.hypothesis: Default is triggered by the trough of operating earnings, not their average, so the distress-relevant quantity is the firm's worst recent operating profit relative to its total obligations; markets extrapolate mean profitability and therefore underprice firms whose downside profitability still covers their liability stock.
input_signals.reasoning: This is no longer the inverse of net-debt/EBITDA: the numerator is a left-tail (three-year minimum) profitability state rather than a level or smoothed mean, which is a genuinely distress-conditioned way of measuring profitability. Scaling by total liabilities instead of interest-bearing debt removes the exploding-denominator fragility for zero-debt firms, since every firm has non-trivial liabilities, so winsorization is a mild guard rather than the source of the signal.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( ts_min( oibdp, 3 ), lt ), 1 )

input_signals.name: ObligationGrowthOutpacingProfit
input_signals.hypothesis: Distress is built, not inherited: when a firm's liabilities expand faster than its operating earning power, the incremental obligations are not self-financing and future default risk rises, yet the market treats liability-funded expansion as growth rather than as deteriorating solvency capacity.
input_signals.reasoning: Rather than swapping the denominator of the archived coverage ratio, this compares the *flows* of the two themes — asset-scaled liability accumulation versus asset-scaled profit accumulation — so the signal is high only when obligations grow without matching profit support, an imbalance neither a leverage level nor a profit-change sort captures. Using asset-scaled first differences instead of growth rates avoids the exploding ratios that plague GROWTH(oibdp) for firms with near-zero or negative base earnings.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( ind_rank( ratio( delta( lt, 1 ), at ) ), ind_rank( ratio( delta( oibdp, 1 ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: MarginCompressionUnderObligations
input_signals.hypothesis: Rising unit cost of sales erodes the cash flow pledged against fixed claims, so gross-margin compression is a leading indicator of default risk only for obligation-heavy firms; the market reads margin drift as an operating detail and misses its solvency implication where there is no slack to absorb it.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the net-debt-issuance-adjacent flow diagnostic with a cost-side margin channel that no archived signal touches, and it conditions on obligations rather than adding another debt-growth leg. The signed carrier is the centered change in cost intensity and the weight is a non-negative leverage rank, so improving-margin levered firms are long, compressing-margin levered firms are short, and debt-free firms sit near the middle; coverage should be high since only cogs, sale, lt and at are required.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( neg( ind_zscore( delta( ratio( cogs, sale ), 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: RolloverPressureAgainstProfit
input_signals.hypothesis: If the working-capital result is really about near-term funding risk, the active ingredient should be current debt rather than the full act−lct netting: profitable firms carrying heavy short-maturity debt must repeatedly return to credit markets, and that rollover exposure is not compensated in equity prices.
input_signals.reasoning: This decomposes Signal 1's mechanism by isolating the maturity-structure component of the liability side, so the pair jointly identifies whether the effect is a liquid-asset buffer story or a short-term-obligation story — an attribution the archive cannot currently make. The construction (centered distress carrier × non-negative profitability rank) is the one that has evaluated cleanly and keeps unprofitable firms muted, where rollover risk is already visibly priced.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( neg( ind_zscore( ratio( dlc, at ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: DebtServiceableCashAfterWorkingCapital
input_signals.hypothesis: Operating profit overstates the cash actually available to service obligations because growth in working capital absorbs it; the distress-relevant quantity is profit net of working-capital investment relative to total liabilities, and firms whose reported profitability is not truly available for debt service are overvalued.
input_signals.reasoning: This keeps the winning obligation-coverage frame but changes its economic content: the numerator is free cash available for fixed claims rather than accounting profit, so the signal separates firms whose earnings genuinely reduce default risk from those whose earnings are trapped in receivables and inventory. It uses only oibdp, wcap and lt, so coverage should match or exceed the TS_MIN-based winner while adding a cash-conversion dimension the archive lacks.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( oibdp, delta( wcap, 1 ) ), lt ), 1 )

input_signals.name: MaturityMixAgainstProfit
input_signals.expression: MUL(NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dltt, dlc)))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What makes profitability valuable is not the amount of debt but how soon it must be repaid: profitable firms that have termed out their borrowing are insulated from credit-market closures, while profitable firms funding themselves at the short end are exposed to rollover risk that equity prices do not discount.
input_signals.reasoning: This holds leverage quantity fixed and varies only the maturity mix, so it separates the winner's mechanism (rollover exposure) from a simple scaled-debt effect, which the archive cannot currently distinguish because dlc/at mixes both. If the maturity-share version retains the fmb ≈ 3.9 / alpha ≈ 4% profile, the mechanism is genuinely refinancing risk; if it collapses, the winner was about debt quantity and the modulator was doing the work.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( neg( ind_zscore( ratio( dlc, add( dltt, dlc ) ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: GrossProfitCoverageOfNearTermClaims
input_signals.hypothesis: Solvency at the relevant horizon is whether one year of gross profit can retire the claims that actually come due; firms whose near-term obligations are small relative to their gross profit flow face negligible refinancing risk and are underpriced relative to that safety.
input_signals.reasoning: This tests whether the multiplicative conditional structure is necessary at all, or whether directly scaling profitability by *near-term* obligations captures the same economics more robustly — the level analogue of the winner, and a sharper version of WorstCaseObligationCoverage (which used total liabilities and delivered 2.61 / +1.7%). It is parsimonious, uses only revt, cogs and lct, and its comparison with Signal 1 pins down whether the effect is coverage-level or conditional-slope in nature.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), lct ), 1 )

input_signals.name: RolloverShockAgainstProfit
input_signals.hypothesis: A profitable firm that is suddenly shifting its funding to the short end is being rationed by long-term lenders, so the *increase* in current-debt intensity is a live warning of financing stress that the market reads as ordinary working-capital borrowing.
input_signals.reasoning: This changes the winner from a state to a flow, which distinguishes a persistent capital-structure characteristic (possibly a risk-premium story spanned by known maturity effects) from a genuine news-based mispricing about deteriorating credit access. The design is deliberately identical in every other respect so the level-versus-change comparison is clean, and coverage should be close to 0.14 since only one lag is added.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( neg( ind_zscore( delta( ratio( dlc, at ), 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: ProfitPremiumInDeficitFirms
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms carrying accumulated retained-earnings deficits are priced as chronic distress cases regardless of current performance, so the operating-profitability premium should be strongest exactly there, where profitability is the variable that resolves survival, and weakest among firms whose long earnings record already reassures investors.
input_signals.reasoning: CurrentProfitVersusLossHistory (alpha +1.8%, t 2.10) showed the current-versus-cumulative profitability gap is priced, but a rank difference cannot say whether the effect is a genuine conditional slope or just two additive channels; this multiplicative form isolates the interaction by muting firms with strong retained earnings. It uses only oibdp, re and at, so coverage should stay near 0.14, and it delivers a lesson that none of the rollover-family signals in this batch can provide.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_zscore( ratio( oibdp, at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( re, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: HardVersusSoftNearTermClaims
input_signals.hypothesis: Not all claims due within a year are equally dangerous: bank and market debt is a hard claim whose non-payment triggers default, whereas payables and accruals are soft claims that roll with ongoing supplier relationships, so for profitable firms it is the *hardness* of near-term claims, not their quantity, that determines true distress risk.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a genuinely new claim about claim quality — orthogonal to quantity (dlc/at), maturity mix (dlc/(dltt+dlc)) and coverage (gp/lct) — and it discriminates a trade-credit story from a default-trigger story, which the archive cannot currently do. If hardness is what matters, this should match or beat the winner; if the effect is really about total near-term claim size, it will weaken, which is itself decisive information for the remaining generations.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( neg( ind_zscore( ratio( dlc, lct ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: ProfitPersistenceOffsetsRolloverRisk
input_signals.hypothesis: Lenders and investors distinguish poorly between firms that have earned operating profits every year and firms that earn them intermittently, yet only the former can reliably roll short-maturity debt; profit *persistence* therefore offsets rollover risk, and its value is concentrated among firms with heavy current debt.
input_signals.reasoning: This is a genuinely different profitability construct — a five-year count of profitable years, not a level, change, trough or second moment — and it directly implements the mandate's "profitability offsets distress" channel on the near-term claim dimension that the archive has shown to matter. The count is centered by industry so both legs are populated among short-debt-heavy firms (long = consistently profitable, short = intermittently profitable), and unlevered-at-the-short-end firms are muted.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ind_zscore( ts_sum( indicator( oiadp, 0 ), 5 ) ), rank( ratio( dlc, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: UnstableNearTermSafetyMargin
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters for refinancing is not only the average size of the safety margin but its reliability: a firm whose gross-profit-to-current-claims ratio swings widely can find itself uncovered exactly when credit tightens, so instability in the coverage margin is a distress characteristic distinct from its level.
input_signals.reasoning: This measures the second moment of the cross-theme coverage margin itself, which is not a smoothing variant of any archived signal but a different statistic with a different economic claim — margin uncertainty rather than margin size — and it is orthogonal to the level ratio that already scores well. Industry-centering makes the sort comparable across sectors with different working-capital cycles, and the five-year window puts expected coverage near 0.12, in line with other window-based signals in the archive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: neg( ind_zscore( winsor( vol( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), lct ), 5 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: RevenueScaleCoverageControl
input_signals.hypothesis: If the near-term coverage effect is genuinely about profitability offsetting distress, then replacing gross profit with revenue — same claims denominator, no margin content — should weaken the result substantially; if instead pure operating scale relative to maturing claims does the work, the discovery is a turnover effect rather than a profitability × distress interaction.
input_signals.reasoning: GrossProfitCoverageOfNearTermClaims delivers fmb 3.25 and α +3.8%, but the critic correctly noted it is gross profitability times inverse short-liability intensity, and nothing in the archive separates the margin channel from the scale channel. This control is cheap, high-coverage and decisive for how the last generations should allocate effort, and it remains a legitimate cross-theme signal in its own right.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: winsor( ratio( revt, lct ), 1 )

input_signals.name: AdditiveProfitVersusHardClaims
input_signals.hypothesis: If the profitability and hard-claim channels enter returns additively, a rank difference should capture the effect as well as the product; if the effect is genuinely conditional — profitability mattering more where hard claims are heavy and vice versa — the multiplicative form should dominate.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's strongest result uses a multiplicative structure but has never been benchmarked against the additive combination of the identical ingredients, so this isolates operator structure alone and directly tests whether the interaction claim is doing economic work. Rank differences have evaluated cleanly here (ObligationGrowthOutpacingProfit reached |t| 4.15 in FMB), so the comparison is fair rather than handicapped by construction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( ratio( dlc, lct ) ) )

input_signals.name: MarginCushionAgainstHardClaims
input_signals.hypothesis: What lets a firm survive maturing hard claims is the cushion between price and cost: a high gross margin means demand or input shocks can be absorbed before the firm turns cash-negative, whereas a low-margin firm with the same asset-scaled profitability is one shock away from being unable to service claims.
input_signals.reasoning: Gross margin (gp/sale) is not a smoothed version of asset-scaled profitability (gp/at) but its orthogonal factor — the two differ by asset turnover — so this adjudicates whether the interaction runs through pricing-power cushion or capital productivity, a question the archive has never separated. Together with the accepted revenue-scale control it completes a clean decomposition of the winning coverage effect into margin, turnover and scale components, using only high-coverage items.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( neg( ind_zscore( ratio( dlc, lct ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), sale ) ) )

input_signals.name: ClaimSizeAndHardnessVersusProfit
input_signals.expression: SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lct), RATIO(lct, at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Near-term claim risk has two separate dimensions — how *hard* the maturing claims are (bank debt versus trade credit) and how *large* they are relative to the firm — and profitability must be compared against both; a profitable firm with a small, mostly-soft claim book is genuinely safe, while claim hardness alone understates risk for firms whose current book is enormous.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's best joint result is the rank difference between gross profitability and hard-claim share (fmb 4.82, α +3.6%), but claim *intensity* has only ever appeared as a modulator, where it performed badly for portfolio-composition reasons; putting it inside the ranked distress side instead tests whether the two claim dimensions are complements. Both inputs are bounded ranks, so this should preserve the strong cross-sectional slope rather than reintroducing skew.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( sumrank( ratio( dlc, lct ), ratio( lct, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: ProfitRankVersusNetHardClaimRank
input_signals.expression: SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), lct)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cash extinguishes maturing debt, so the distress side of the profitability comparison should be hard claims *net* of cash; ranking that net measure prevents cash-rich outliers from dominating while preserving the economic content that a firm holding cash against its short debt bears no rollover risk.
input_signals.reasoning: NetHardClaimShareAgainstProfit delivered α +4.5% (t 3.81) with FMB −1.25, the same skew signature as the other cash-based carrier, so this places the identical economic quantity inside the rank-difference structure that produced the archive's best cross-sectional evidence. Comparing it against Signal 2 also separates whether cash is best treated as a debt offset or as a standalone liquidity buffer, which is the remaining open question in this family before the final generation.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( ratio( sub( dlc, che ), lct ) ) )

input_signals.name: WeakestLinkSafetyScore
input_signals.hypothesis: Survival is governed by the binding constraint, not by an average: a firm is only as safe as its weaker dimension, so a highly profitable firm with hard maturing debt and an unprofitable firm with soft claims should both be classified as risky, and only firms strong on *both* dimensions should command the safety premium.
input_signals.reasoning: A minimum is not a monotone transform of either the sum or the product — it is a non-smooth aggregator that deliberately refuses to let strength on one dimension compensate for weakness on the other — so it makes a distinct economic claim about how distress risk aggregates rather than restating the archived product with a different standardization. Comparing it against the additive rank difference (fmb 4.82, α +3.6%) and the centered-carrier product (fmb 4.15, α +4.0%) tells us whether the mechanism is compensatory or constraint-driven, which is the substantive question behind all three forms.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( dlc, lct ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: WeakestLinkNetOfCash
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(dlc, che), lct))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm is only as safe as its weaker dimension, and the correct measure of the claim dimension is hard maturing debt *net of the cash that can extinguish it*; a firm that is profitable and whose cash already covers its short debt has no binding constraint, while failing either test leaves it exposed.
input_signals.reasoning: This unites the two independently validated gen-7 improvements — the weakest-link aggregator (best fmb 4.91 and Sharpe 0.333) and the cash-netted hard-claim rank (best alpha +5.3%, t 4.76) — each of which improved a different metric relative to the parent design, so the combination targets joint strength rather than one dimension. Both legs are bounded industry ranks, so the skew that broke the FMB slopes of raw cash carriers cannot reappear, and coverage should hold at ≈0.124.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( sub( dlc, che ), lct ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: TripleConstraintSafety
input_signals.expression: MIN(MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dlc, lct)))), IND_RANK(RATIO(che, lct)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Survival requires earning power, soft maturing claims, and a liquid reserve simultaneously; if any one of the three is weak the firm is exposed regardless of the other two, so the safety premium should accrue only to firms clearing all three constraints.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive shows all three ingredients matter separately, but nothing tells us how many constraints must bind at once; adding cash coverage as a third weakest-link component answers that and directly tests whether the top decile becomes more sharply defined (higher alpha) or merely narrower and noisier (lower t-stat). It is the natural next step from Signal 1 and its comparison with it is the informative part.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( min( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( dlc, lct ) ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( che, lct ) ) )

input_signals.name: WeakestLinkOnDebtIntensity
input_signals.hypothesis: If the binding claim constraint is the *quantity* of maturing debt relative to the firm rather than its share of the current book, then scaling short debt by assets should preserve or improve the weakest-link result while covering firms whose current liabilities are small or unreported.
input_signals.reasoning: The two claim measures have never been compared inside the weakest-link structure, and dlc/at was the carrier with the archive's widest coverage (0.144 versus 0.125), so this simultaneously tests the economic question and the robustness of the leading result to a broader sample. A materially higher coverage with comparable statistics would make this the preferred final specification.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( dlc, at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DownsideProfitWeakestLink
input_signals.hypothesis: The profitability constraint binds in bad years, not average ones, so the relevant earning-power leg of a binding-constraint safety score is the firm's worst recent operating income; a firm whose trough profitability is still healthy and whose maturing claims are mostly soft has no state in which it is forced to the credit market.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the arithmetic complement of the leading signal with a genuine candidate that keeps the validated weakest-link aggregator but upgrades the profitability leg from a current-year level to a realized downside state, which oiadp can express because it goes negative for a substantial share of firm-years. It also gives the trough concept a fair test inside the structure that works, after the ratio form (TroughOperatingIncomeOverClaims) failed at α −0.7% while the same trough idea in the total-liability frame had earlier scored fmb 2.61.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( ts_min( oiadp, 3 ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( dlc, lct ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: NetCurrentClaimWeakestLink
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(lct, che), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: If what binds is the total settlement obligation coming due within the year rather than only its hard bank-debt component, then all current liabilities net of cash should be the correct claim leg, since payables and accruals must also ultimately be funded from operations.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive established that *near-term* claims dominate total leverage, but never resolved whether hardness (dlc) or the full current book (lct) is the binding measure once cash is netted out — the hard-versus-soft test was run only in the multiplicative form. Holding the aggregator, the profitability leg and the asset scaler fixed makes this a clean one-variable adjudication of the central economic claim of the whole research line.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( sub( lct, che ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: BottomLineProfitWeakestLink
input_signals.hypothesis: If the profitability leg of the safety score works because it measures genuine debt-servicing capacity rather than because gross profitability is a known return predictor, then replacing gross profit with operating income after depreciation — a measure net of overhead and capital consumption — should preserve or improve the result.
input_signals.reasoning: Every strong signal in the archive uses revt−cogs, so the finding is vulnerable to the charge that it is Novy-Marx gross profitability wearing a distress costume; oiadp is economically the cash claim-servicing measure and is only weakly correlated with gross profit in the cross-section. The trough version of oiadp inside this aggregator already produced fmb 3.10 and α +3.1%, so the current-level version is the natural and final robustness test of the profitability leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( oiadp, at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( sub( dlc, che ), lct ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: MarginAsThirdBindingConstraint
input_signals.expression: MIN(MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(dlc, lct)))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), sale)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Survival requires earning power, soft maturing claims, and a pricing cushion: a firm with thin margins converts any cost or demand shock straight into a funding shortfall, so the margin should act as a third constraint that binds independently of asset-scaled profitability and claim structure.
input_signals.reasoning: Adding cash as a third constraint kept the alpha at +5.2% with a t of 4.74, showing the aggregator tolerates a third leg; margin is the more orthogonal candidate because gp/at equals margin times asset turnover, and the margin channel independently produced α +3.6% (t 3.59) in the product form. This tests whether the pricing cushion adds a genuinely separate binding dimension or merely narrows the long leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( min( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( dlc, lct ) ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), sale ) ) )

input_signals.name: TotalNetDebtWeakestLink
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The alternative to the near-term thesis is that total net indebtedness is what binds against earning power, with maturity structure irrelevant once cash is netted out; under that view long-term debt is an equally hard claim because it must eventually be refinanced.
input_signals.reasoning: This is the decisive falsification test for the thesis that has driven the last five generations — that *short-dated* claims, not total leverage, are what interact with profitability — because it changes only the maturity content of the claim leg while holding the aggregator, cash-netting, scaler and profitability leg identical to Signal 1. A materially weaker result confirms the near-term mechanism; a comparable result would mean the discovery is about net indebtedness generally, which is important to know before reporting the final specification.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( sub( add( dltt, dlc ), che ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: DebtServiceWeakestLink
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at)), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dlc, xint), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: What creditors actually demand each year is maturing principal *plus* interest, so the binding claim constraint is the total annual debt-service call on the firm rather than a stock of short debt; a firm whose earning power is strong and whose yearly service demand is small has no constraint that binds, while a high service call makes even profitable firms dependent on credit markets.
input_signals.reasoning: This changes the economic content of the claim leg from a balance-sheet stock to a cash-service flow — adding the interest component, which embeds the price lenders charge and has never appeared inside the weakest-link aggregator — so the outcome is not predictable from the cash-netting or asset-scaling parents. It also revives the credit-cost channel (LenderRateVersusReportedProfit, α +1.6%, t 1.98) in the structure that has proven able to convert weak channels into strong ones, at coverage comparable to the dlc/at family.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ratio( add( dlc, xint ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: PeakShortDebtRelianceWeakestLink
input_signals.hypothesis: Fiscal-year-end balance sheets understate true funding practice because firms pay down revolvers before the reporting date; the firm's *peak* short-debt reliance over the past three years reveals how hard it actually leans on the short end, and only firms that have never leaned hard, and are profitable, are genuinely unconstrained.
input_signals.reasoning: Unlike the lagged-score duration idea, a three-year maximum of the claim ratio is not close to a monotone transform of its current value — it is precisely the firms whose current snapshot looks clean but whose history does not that get reclassified, which is where the measurement error in short-debt reporting lives. It keeps the validated aggregator and profitability leg fixed so the test isolates snapshot-versus-peak measurement of the binding claim, at a coverage cost of only two extra years of history.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( sub( revt, cogs ), at ) ), ind_rank( neg( ts_max( ratio( dlc, lct ), 3 ) ) ) )
